1. FIFO Page Replacement Algorithm

The First-In, First-Out (FIFO) Page Replacement Algorithm is one of the simplest memory management techniques used by operating systems to manage virtual memory. Under FIFO, the operating system maintains a queue of all pages currently residing in physical memory frames. When a page fault occurs and a page must be replaced, the algorithm selects the page that has been in memory the longest—that is, the page at the head of the FIFO queue. Once selected, the old page is swapped out (or discarded if clean), the new page is loaded into the freed frame, and its reference is appended to the tail of the queue. While FIFO is computationally lightweight with an \(O(1)\) replacement complexity and requires minimal hardware support, it suffers from a major performance flaw: it ignores page reference frequency and recency. A heavily accessed page loaded early in execution is just as vulnerable to eviction as an unreferenced initialization page.

2. Belady's Anomaly

In most intuitive caching and memory systems, increasing physical memory (i.e., providing more page frames) should monotonically decrease or at least keep constant the total number of page faults. However, in 1969, Laszlo Belady discovered that under certain non-stack page replacement algorithms like FIFO, increasing the number of allocated frames can actually increase the number of page faults for specific page reference sequences. This counter-intuitive behavior is known as Belady's Anomaly.

Algorithms that are susceptible to Belady's Anomaly fail to satisfy the inclusion property. The inclusion property dictates that the set of pages present in an \(n\)-frame memory system at any time step \(t\) must always be a subset of the pages present in an \((n+1)\)-frame system at the same time step: \[ S_n(t) \subseteq S_{n+1}(t) \] Algorithms satisfying this property (such as LRU and Optimal) are termed Stack Algorithms and are mathematically proven to never exhibit Belady's Anomaly.

3. Concrete Numerical Example of Belady's Anomaly

Consider the famous reference string: \(1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\).

  • Case A: 3 Page Frames

    Execution trace yields 9 Page Faults. The frames evolve as follows:

    • Ref 1: [1, -, -] (Fault 1)
    • Ref 2: [1, 2, -] (Fault 2)
    • Ref 3: [1, 2, 3] (Fault 3)
    • Ref 4: [4, 2, 3] (Fault 4, evicts 1)
    • Ref 1: [4, 1, 3] (Fault 5, evicts 2)
    • Ref 2: [4, 1, 2] (Fault 6, evicts 3)
    • Ref 5: [5, 1, 2] (Fault 7, evicts 4)
    • Ref 1: [5, 1, 2] (Hit)
    • Ref 2: [5, 1, 2] (Hit)
    • Ref 3: [5, 3, 2] (Fault 8, evicts 1)
    • Ref 4: [5, 3, 4] (Fault 9, evicts 2)
    • Ref 5: [5, 3, 4] (Hit)
  • Case B: 4 Page Frames

    Increasing frames from 3 to 4 increases page faults to 10 Page Faults:

    • Ref 1..4: [1, 2, 3, 4] (Faults 1, 2, 3, 4)
    • Ref 1, 2: [1, 2, 3, 4] (Hits)
    • Ref 5: [5, 2, 3, 4] (Fault 5, evicts 1)
    • Ref 1: [5, 1, 3, 4] (Fault 6, evicts 2)
    • Ref 2: [5, 1, 2, 4] (Fault 7, evicts 3)
    • Ref 3: [5, 1, 2, 3] (Fault 8, evicts 4)
    • Ref 4: [4, 1, 2, 3] (Fault 9, evicts 5)
    • Ref 5: [4, 5, 2, 3] (Fault 10, evicts 1)

1. Overview of Least Recently Used (LRU) Algorithm

The Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement algorithm is a heuristic approximation of the theoretical Optimal Page Replacement algorithm. LRU is based on the principle of temporal locality: pages that have been referenced recently are highly likely to be referenced again in the near future. Conversely, the page that has not been referenced for the longest period of time is selected for eviction when a page fault occurs. Unlike FIFO, LRU is a stack algorithm, meaning it is mathematically immune to Belady's Anomaly. The inclusion property \(S_n(t) \subseteq S_{n+1}(t)\) holds at all execution steps.

2. Implementation Strategies

Implementing true LRU requires tracking the reference history of every allocated frame, which poses non-trivial hardware and software overhead. The main approaches include:

  • Counters / Logical Clock Implementation:

    The CPU maintains a global 64-bit logical clock/counter that increments with every memory instruction. Each page table entry includes a hardware field called the Time-of-Use. On every memory access, the current counter value is copied into the accessed page's Time-of-Use field. When a page fault occurs, the OS scans the page table to find the entry with the smallest timestamp \(t_{min} = \min_{i} (\text{Timestamp}_i)\). This method incurs an \(O(N)\) search penalty unless min-heap structures are maintained, and requires clock update support on every instruction execution.

  • Doubly Linked List + Hash Map (LRU Cache Architecture):

    In software/OS kernel implementations, LRU is efficiently structured using a Doubly Linked List combined with a Hash Map:

    • The Doubly Linked List maintains page frames ordered by recency of access. The Most Recently Used (MRU) page resides at the head, and the Least Recently Used (LRU) page resides at the tail.
    • The Hash Map maps a Frame Number/Page ID to its corresponding node pointer in the doubly linked list.
    • On a memory hit, the referenced node is located in \(O(1)\) via the hash table and moved to the head of the list in \(O(1)\) time.
    • On a page fault, the tail node (LRU page) is evicted, removed from both list and hash table in \(O(1)\), and the newly loaded page is inserted at the head.
  • Hardware Approximation: Clock Algorithm (Second Chance):

    Because updating pointers or timestamps on every single memory reference in hardware is expensive, modern operating systems use hardware-assisted approximations such as the Clock Algorithm. Each frame possesses a 1-bit Reference Bit set to 1 by hardware on access. A circular pointer sweeps frames like a clock hand: if a frame's reference bit is 1, it is cleared to 0 (given a second chance); if it is 0, the frame is selected for replacement.

1. Concept and Theoretical Foundation

The Optimal Page Replacement Algorithm (also known as OPT, MIN, or Belady's Optimal Algorithm) replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. Formally, if memory currently contains frames \(F = \{p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k\}\), and the future access time for page \(p_i\) is given by \(t_{next}(p_i)\), OPT selects page \(p^*\) for eviction such that: \[ p^* = \arg\max_{p_i \in F} \left( t_{next}(p_i) \right) \] OPT provides the absolute minimum page fault rate for any fixed frame allocation and page reference stream. Because it relies on knowledge of future events, it belongs to the class of stack algorithms and is completely immune to Belady's Anomaly.

2. Impossibility of Real-Time Implementation and Practical Utility

OPT is classified as an offline algorithm or oracle-based algorithm. In a general-purpose operating system, the future memory access stream of executing processes cannot be predicted deterministically, making OPT unrealizable in real-time runtime environments.

Despite its unfeasibility for live systems, OPT plays a critical role in operating system research and design:

  • It serves as an upper bound / benchmark against which all practical, online page replacement algorithms (such as LRU, FIFO, Clock, and LFU) are evaluated.
  • It can be simulated offline by recording execution trace logs during a test run and replaying the trace to compute the theoretical baseline performance.

3. Step-by-Step Execution Example

Consider a system with 3 page frames and the reference string: \(7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3\).

  • Ref 7, 0, 1: Initial loads fill frames \([7, 0, 1]\). (3 Faults)
  • Ref 2: Page Fault. Look ahead into future: 0 is used at step 5, 1 is not used again soon, 7 is never used. Evict 7. Memory becomes \([2, 0, 1]\). (Fault 4)
  • Ref 0: Hit in frame \([2, 0, 1]\).
  • Ref 3: Page Fault. Look ahead: 0 is used next (step 7), 2 is used at step 9, 1 is not used again. Evict 1. Memory becomes \([2, 0, 3]\). (Fault 5)
  • Ref 0: Hit in frame \([2, 0, 3]\).
  • Ref 4: Page Fault. Look ahead: 2 is used at step 9, 3 is used at step 10, 0 is not used. Evict 0. Memory becomes \([2, 4, 3]\). (Fault 6)
  • Ref 2, 3: Hits in memory. Total page faults = 6.

1. The Thrashing Phenomenon

Thrashing is a severe operating system performance degradation state wherein the CPU spends significantly more time performing page swapping (I/O operations) than executing actual process instructions. Thrashing occurs when the total memory footprint demanded by active processes exceeds the available physical RAM frames in the system.

The mechanics of thrashing follow a vicious feedback loop:

  1. As the degree of multiprogramming (number of active processes in memory) increases, physical frames allocated per process decrease.
  2. Processes frequently experience page faults because their active code/data pages are evicted.
  3. Processes enter the I/O waiting queue to fetch faulted pages from disk, causing overall CPU utilization to plummet.
  4. The OS CPU scheduler observes low CPU utilization and incorrectly infers that system load is light, prompting it to launch even more processes (further increasing multiprogramming).
  5. System throughput drops to near zero while paging disk activity hits 100% saturation.

2. The Working Set Model

To eliminate thrashing, Peter Denning introduced the Working Set Model based on the principle of locality of reference. A process does not access its entire address space uniformly; instead, it moves through distinct execution phases (localities) where it repeatedly references a small subset of pages.

Key parameters of the model include:

  • Working Set Window (\(\Delta\)): A fixed number of recent page references (e.g., \(\Delta = 10,000\) references).
  • Working Set of Process \(P_i\) (\(WSS_i\)): The set of distinct pages referenced by process \(P_i\) within the most recent \(\Delta\) time window: \[ WSS_i(t, \Delta) = \{ \text{pages referenced by } P_i \text{ in time interval } [t - \Delta, t] \} \]
  • Total System Demand (\(D\)): The sum of working set sizes across all \(n\) active processes: \[ D = \sum_{i=1}^{n} WSS_i \]

3. Prevention of Thrashing via Working Set Control

Let \(m\) be the total number of available physical RAM frames in the system. The operating system monitors \(D\) continuously:

  • If \(D \le m\), physical memory can satisfy the locality requirements of all active processes, and execution proceeds smoothly.
  • If \(D > m\), system demand exceeds physical memory. Thrashing is imminent. The operating system must select one or more processes, suspend their execution, and swap their allocated frames out to disk until \(D \le m\) is restored.

1. Introduction to File Allocation Methods

File allocation methods dictate how operating systems assign secondary storage disk blocks to store file data. The choice of allocation scheme directly impacts disk space utilization, sequential/direct access performance, and directory entry overhead. The three classical allocation strategies are Contiguous Allocation, Linked Allocation, and Indexed Allocation.

2. Detailed Comparative Analysis

  • Contiguous Allocation:

    Each file occupies a set of contiguous physical blocks on disk. A file starting at block \(b\) and of length \(n\) occupies blocks \(b, b+1, b+2, \dots, b+n-1\). The directory entry simply stores \((b, n)\).

    • Advantages: Superior I/O throughput due to minimal disk head movement; supports extremely fast direct/random access where block address \(b_k = b + k\) in \(O(1)\) time.
    • Disadvantages: Severe external fragmentation requiring periodic disk compaction; difficult to handle dynamic file growth without pre-allocating large unused buffers.
  • Linked Allocation:

    Each file is represented as a linked list of disk blocks scattered anywhere on disk. Each block contains file data plus a pointer (e.g., 4 bytes) to the next physical block. The directory entry stores pointers to the First and Last blocks.

    • Advantages: Completely eliminates external fragmentation; files can grow dynamically as long as free blocks exist.
    • Disadvantages: Poor random access performance (\(O(N)\) pointer traversals required to reach block \(k\)); disk space overhead for storing pointers; vulnerability to reliability issues (a corrupted pointer breaks the file chain). Note: The File Allocation Table (FAT) variant moves pointers to a central memory table to accelerate lookup.
  • Indexed Allocation:

    Brings all file pointers together into a dedicated data structure called an Index Block (or Inode). The directory entry points directly to the index block, which contains an array of pointers to the actual data blocks.

    • Advantages: Supports fast random access (\(O(1)\) lookup in index array) without external fragmentation.
    • Disadvantages: Pointer overhead for very small files (allocates a full index block even for 1-byte files). Large files require multi-level indexing (single, double, or triple indirect blocks).

1. Overview of Directory Organization

A directory structure is an essential operating system component that organizes file system metadata, providing user access control, namespace isolation, logical grouping, and fast searching capabilities. The architecture of file directories evolved from primitive flat models to complex hierarchical tree and graph structures.

2. Classification of Directory Structures

  • Single-Level Directory:

    The simplest structure where all files reside in a single root directory shared by all users on the system.

    • Pros & Cons: Easy to implement and search on small systems. However, it suffers from severe naming collisions (every file must have a unique name) and offers zero logical grouping or user isolation, making it unviable for multi-user systems.
  • Two-Level Directory:

    Introduces isolation by creating a Master User Directory (MUD) at the top level, which points to individual User File Directories (UFDs) for each user account.

    • Pros & Cons: Solves the global naming collision problem because different users can create files with identical names (e.g., `/UserA/test.c` vs `/UserB/test.c`). However, users cannot create subfolders within their UFDs, preventing fine-grained hierarchical file organization.
  • Tree-Structured Directory:

    Extends directory organization to arbitrary depth hierarchies. Directories are treated as special files that can contain both file nodes and subdirectory nodes branching from a single Root Directory (`/`).

    • Key Concepts:
      • Absolute Pathname: Specifies the full path starting from the root directory (e.g., `/home/user/docs/report.pdf`).
      • Relative Pathname: Specifies path relative to the Current Working Directory (CWD) (e.g., `./docs/report.pdf`).
    • Pros: Excellent organization capabilities, fine-grained access control, and complete protection against unauthorized path traversals.

1. Purpose of Disk Scheduling Algorithms

In hard disk drive (HDD) storage architecture, mechanical head movement across tracks (cylinders) constitutes the primary performance bottleneck. Total disk I/O service time is dominated by Seek Time (moving the read/write head to the targeted cylinder). The primary goal of disk scheduling algorithms is to reorder pending I/O requests in the disk queue to minimize total head movement, reduce average seek latency, and maximize system throughput.

2. Primary Disk Scheduling Algorithms

  • First-Come, First-Served (FCFS):

    Processes requests strictly in the arrival order. It is inherently fair and avoids starvation. However, if requests are scattered across distant cylinders, the disk head swings back and forth wildly (wild head movement), leading to high average seek times.

  • Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF):

    Selects the pending request that requires the minimum head movement from the current cylinder position. While SSTF drastically reduces average seek time compared to FCFS, it is prone to starvation for requests targeting distant cylinders if a steady stream of requests arrives near the current head position.

  • SCAN (Elevator Algorithm):

    The disk arm starts at one end of the disk and moves toward the opposite end, servicing all requests along the path. Upon reaching the final cylinder in that direction, the arm movement direction reverses, servicing requests in the opposite direction. SCAN bounds maximum waiting time and prevents starvation, but favors cylinders near the disk edges over mid-range cylinders.

  • C-SCAN (Circular SCAN):

    Restricts service to one direction only. The disk head moves from cylinder 0 to cylinder \(N\), servicing requests along the way. Upon reaching end \(N\), it immediately wraps back to cylinder 0 without servicing any requests on the return sweep, then repeats. C-SCAN provides a strictly uniform waiting time distribution across all disk cylinders.

3. Comparative Evaluation Example

Given a disk with cylinders 0 to 199, current head position at 53, and request queue: \(98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67\).

  • FCFS Total Seek Distance: \(|53-98| + |98-183| + \dots = 640\) cylinders.
  • SSTF Total Seek Distance: Traverses nearest cylinders first \((53 \to 65 \to 67 \to 37 \to 14 \to 98 \to 122 \to 124 \to 183) = 236\) cylinders.

1. Architecture of the UNIX Inode

In UNIX file systems (e.g., UFS, ext2, ext3), an Inode (Index Node) is a fixed-size control data structure that stores all metadata describing a file or directory, except for its actual filename and path (which are maintained in directory block entries mapping names to inode numbers).

An Inode structure contains essential file metadata, including:

  • File Mode / Type (regular file, directory, symbolic link, character device).
  • Owner Information (User ID - UID, Group ID - GID).
  • Access Permissions (read, write, execute bits for user, group, others).
  • File Size in Bytes.
  • Timestamps: Access Time (\(atime\)), Modification Time (\(mtime\)), and Inode Change Time (\(ctime\)).
  • Hard Link Count (number of directory entries pointing to this inode).
  • Block Pointer Array for allocated file storage.

2. Block Pointer Hierarchy

To efficiently support both small files (with zero pointer overhead) and massive multi-gigabyte files, traditional UNIX inodes utilize an asymmetric multi-level index block structure consisting of 15 pointers:

  • Direct Pointers (Pointers 0 to 11): 12 direct pointers that store the physical block addresses of the first 12 data blocks of the file. Provides instantaneous \(O(1)\) direct access for small files.
  • Single Indirect Pointer (Pointer 12): Points to an index block on disk. This index block contains an array of direct pointers to data blocks.
  • Double Indirect Pointer (Pointer 13): Points to a disk block containing pointers to single indirect blocks, each of which in turn points to data blocks.
  • Triple Indirect Pointer (Pointer 14): Points to a disk block containing pointers to double indirect blocks.

3. Mathematical File Size Calculation

Suppose a UNIX file system has a block size of \(B = 4\text{ KB} = 4096\text{ bytes}\) and disk block pointers of size \(p = 4\text{ bytes}\).

  • Number of pointers per index block: \(K = \frac{B}{p} = \frac{4096}{4} = 1024\) pointers.
  • Direct Storage: \(12 \times 4\text{ KB} = 48\text{ KB}\).
  • Single Indirect Storage: \(1024 \times 4\text{ KB} = 4\text{ MB}\).
  • Double Indirect Storage: \(1024^2 \times 4\text{ KB} = 1024 \times 1024 \times 4\text{ KB} = 4\text{ GB}\).
  • Triple Indirect Storage: \(1024^3 \times 4\text{ KB} = 4\text{ TB}\).
  • Maximum Theoretical File Size: \(48\text{ KB} + 4\text{ MB} + 4\text{ GB} + 4\text{ TB} \approx 4.004\text{ TB}\).

1. Fundamentals of Multithreading

A thread represents the smallest unit of CPU execution within a process, containing its own Program Counter (PC), register set, and stack memory, while sharing address space, global variables, and open file descriptors with sibling threads. Multithreading can be implemented in User Space (User-Level Threads - ULT) or Kernel Space (Kernel-Level Threads - KLT).

2. Architectural Comparison: ULT vs KLT

  • User-Level Threads (ULT):

    ULTs are managed entirely in user space by a runtime thread library (e.g., POSIX Pthreads user implementation, Java Green Threads) without OS kernel awareness. The kernel treats the entire process as a single execution context.

    • Advantages: Thread creation, context switching, and destruction are extremely fast because they require no kernel mode traps or system calls (\(O(1)\) user-space pointer updates); highly portable across operating systems.
    • Disadvantages: If any ULT executes a blocking system call (e.g., synchronous read), the kernel suspends the entire process, blocking all sibling threads; cannot schedule threads concurrently across multiple physical CPU cores.
  • Kernel-Level Threads (KLT):

    KLTs are managed directly by the operating system kernel's native scheduler (e.g., Linux NPTL, Windows Threads). The kernel maintains thread context registers and stacks.

    • Advantages: True parallel execution on multi-core hardware; if one thread blocks on an I/O call, the kernel can independently schedule another thread from the same process.
    • Disadvantages: Higher overhead: context switching between threads requires switching CPU execution privilege modes (user mode to kernel mode trap) and saving/restoring register state.

3. Summary Mapping Models

  • Many-to-One Model: Maps multiple user threads to 1 kernel thread (Pure ULT). Fast, but no true multi-core processing.
  • One-to-One Model: Maps each user thread to 1 kernel thread (Modern Standard: Linux/Windows). Supports full concurrency.
  • Many-to-Many Model: Multiplexes \(M\) user threads over \(N\) kernel threads (\(M \ge N\)). Optimizes resource allocation.

1. System Calls for Process Management in UNIX

In UNIX-like operating systems, process creation, program execution, synchronization, and resource reclamation are mediated by four core system calls: fork(), exec(), wait(), and exit(). Together, they define the complete lifecycle of UNIX processes.

2. Detailed Explanation of System Calls

  • fork() - Process Creation:

    Creates a new child process by spawning a near-identical clone of the calling parent process. The child inherits the parent's environment, file descriptors, CPU registers, and address space.

    • Return Values: Returns 0 inside the newly created child process; returns the child's PID inside the parent process; returns -1 on failure.
    • Optimization: Modern UNIX uses Copy-on-Write (COW): memory pages are shared read-only initially, and only copied when either process attempts a write operation.
  • exec() Family - Program Execution:

    Replaces the current process memory image (code segment, data segment, heap, stack) with a new executable binary file loaded from disk (e.g., execvp("ls", args)). If successful, exec() does not return; execution starts at the main entry point of the new program while retaining the original PID.

  • wait() / waitpid() - Synchronization & Status Retrieval:

    Blocks the calling parent process until one of its child processes terminates. It retrieves the child's termination status exit code and allows the kernel to clean up the child's entry in the process table.

  • exit() - Process Termination:

    Terminates the calling process explicitly (or implicitly upon returning from main). It releases allocated user-space memory, closes file descriptors, sends a SIGCHLD signal to the parent process, and passes an exit status code to the kernel.

3. Process States: Zombies and Orphans

  • Zombie Process: A child process that has executed exit(), but whose parent has not yet called wait(). Its process table entry remains allocated as a `` state until the parent reaps it.
  • Orphan Process: A child process whose parent process terminated before calling wait(). The orphan is automatically adopted by init (PID 1) or systemd, which routinely reaps zombie children.
